On building scalable control planes

I’ve been working at AWS for nearly fourteen years, and for almost all of that time I’ve been building control planes. It’s not the kind of career anyone maps out for themselves. Nobody leaves university thinking “I want to spend the next decade making sure the bookkeeping layer of a cloud service stays up.” But here I am, and I think the reason I’m still here is that control planes turn out to be where many of the interesting problems live, even if it takes a while to see that clearly.

Before Amazon, I worked at a telecoms company in Cape Town where we had maybe ten servers, all in a room in the back of the office, and every single one had a name. You’d SSH into them, you’d share them with your colleagues, and if something went wrong you could walk over and deal with it. That was my entire mental model of what it meant to run infrastructure. Servers were things you knew individually, took care of deliberately, and could reason about as a set because there were few enough to fit in your head.

I mention this not because it’s an unusual background but because it was so common less than two decades ago, and I think that’s what makes it worth saying out loud. Maybe your version is a small Kubernetes cluster or a handful of RDS instances where you can visualize the whole thing, you can name the parts, and when something breaks you know which part broke. That feeling of knowing your infrastructure is comfortable, and it makes the next part of the story genuinely hard to describe, because what happened when I joined EC2 was that that feeling just evaporated.

Honestly, when I started, I didn’t really understand how EC2 worked. I kept trying to map it back to what I knew. If I launch an instance and the underlying server dies, what happens? Does my VM somehow get teleported onto another host? How does the cloud create this illusion that hardware failures don’t matter? I couldn’t square any of it with what I knew about running software.

My first job at EC2 was health-checking the fleet, pinging every server and trying to figure out if it was healthy or not, and what I found was the opposite of magic. Things were failing constantly. Hosts were going down, hardware misbehaving, disks dying. I had seen the underbelly of EC2 and it was chaotic. My mental model had gone from “servers are precious things you protect” to “everything is on fire all the time.”

It took a while to shake that feeling, but what I would eventually come to realize was that these failures were tiny drops in an enormous ocean of things working fine. The system was just operating at a scale where failures were a constant, a statistical certainty rather than an emergency. And the thing that made it possible to run a service at that scale without a human responding to every failure, the thing keeping everything humming, was the control plane.

One way or another, my years at AWS have been spent working on control planes. Every AWS service has one, and I like to think of them as our unsung heroes. The better they work, the less anyone notices them. They’re the reason you don’t have to name your servers, and the reason that when hardware fails, you as a customer never have to deal with it. I’ve gotten to build control planes for two major AWS services: EC2, and DSQL. They’re nearly a decade apart, yet the hard lessons from building one led directly to the design of the other, and that’s the story I want to tell today.

What is a control plane anyway?

At this point, I probably owe you a better explanation of what I mean by control plane and why I think they’re interesting. I’ll use EC2 as an example, because that’s where I learned most of what I know.

The way I think about it is that every service has a data plane and a control plane. The data plane is the set of core capabilities, the raw computing power, the hardware, the networking. The control plane is the conduit between those capabilities and customers. It’s the thing that takes what exists physically in a data center and presents it to you in a format you can actually consume and get value from. Without the control plane, you’d be back to SSH-ing into named servers in a closet somewhere. With it, you can spin up a thousand machines with an API call and never think about where they live.

EC2 involves thousands of engineers and more features than anyone can keep track of, and yet the control plane, conceptually… is pretty simple. Stripped down, EC2 lets you rent a virtual machine (VM) in the cloud, and the control plane’s job is to set up and tear down these VMs for you.

I like the analogy of a thermostat, because it’s constantly measuring the temperature, it knows where things need to be, and it’s always nudging the system in the right direction. That’s what our control plane does. It’s a continuous loop, watching the state of the world, comparing it to what should be true, and correcting the difference. When you launch a VM, the control plane records that a VM should exist, finds a physical server in the right data center, sets up the image, configures networking, and launches it. Later, if that server disappears for any reason, the control plane notices and updates its records to reflect reality. It’s always reconciling what is with what should be.

One thing the team talked about constantly, almost to the point where it became a mantra, was that no matter what happens to the control plane, VMs that are already running need to keep working. We call this static stability, and it sounds obvious because of course running VMs should keep running. But at scale, obvious things are the hardest to protect, because every new feature, every change, every dependency is a chance to accidentally violate that guarantee. Maintaining it is the difference between an outage where customers can’t launch new resources and an outage where everything stops. Both are bad, but the second is catastrophically worse. The fact that EC2 was statically stable gave me some comfort in my early days.

The EC2 team has done a phenomenal job making bad days rare. But understanding what bad days look like shaped a lot of what I know about building control planes.

Living inside the control plane

To understand how bad days start, it helps to know how the control plane stores state. At the heart of EC2’s control plane there is a relational database. When customers call the RunInstances API to launch a VM, the most critical thing that happens is that the control plane writes a row into its database: customer X now has VM Y. That’s when the API can safely return.

In reality, a single RunInstances request triggers hundreds or thousands of internal API calls between micro and macro-services. Many of these services have their own databases recording their own state. It’s hard to exaggerate how complex this has grown over the years, but at the very bottom of all that complexity, there is a MySQL database, and what’s in that database is supposed to match reality.

The simplest way things went wrong was also the scariest. Sometimes the primary database server just died. Our solution was a hot standby, a backup server continuously replicating from the primary, ideally only milliseconds behind. When the primary failed, we’d cut over to the standby and it could limit the outage to seconds. The team earned that through years of operational practice, building tooling, writing runbooks, training on-call engineers to execute the switchover under pressure. But seconds of outage still meant pagers getting lit up at 3am and asking humans to make decisions with incomplete information. We kept asking ourselves whether the architecture could take humans out of that loop entirely.

The slower, more chronic problem was making sure our MySQL database kept up with business growth. This is pretty frustrating when you think about it, because the data plane does all the heavy lifting, like downloading VM images, configuring networking, running workloads, while the database is just keeping track of what exists. Every instance we launched meant more inserts, more updates, and more reads against the database, and eventually the bookkeeper couldn’t keep up with the workers.

So we introduced more servers replicating from the primary and used these as read replicas. Many of the EC2 APIs don’t make any changes, they just describe the state of your current resources (how many VMs do you have, and so on). We sent traffic for these read-only APIs to our new read replicas and this massively reduced the load on our primary database server. This is standard practice for any team trying to scale up a relational database. Incidentally, this fleet of read replicas is why the EC2 API is eventually consistent, and as Marc Brooker has written, this puts an unfortunate cognitive load on our customers. It’s something we wanted to do better with DSQL, which we’ll get to in a bit.

Read replicas bought us time, but every write still funneled through a single primary server, and eventually we had to shard the database. The first phase of this was visible to customers as we split each AWS region into multiple availability zones (AZs), each with their own independent control plane and separate MySQL databases. This helped with both scaling and availability, since zones fail independently and the blast radius of any single failure shrinks. It also became a fundamental building block that allows AWS customers to build architectures resilient to the loss of a single AZ. The second phase was internal: we sharded each zone into what we call cells. Both of these projects took years of engineering time because they required changes across many services. Every place in the codebase that talks to the database has to know which shard to route to. Simple lookups by primary key are straightforward, but anything else, such as joins across data that doesn’t align with your sharding boundaries, gets much trickier. Even the simplest decisions have consequences at this level. Do you shard by account or by resource? Different services choose differently depending on their access patterns, and there’s no universally right answer.

There is also a human cost to all of this that I don’t think we talk about enough. In those early years, we didn’t have the automation to handle a lot of what a modern control plane just takes care of. When a security vulnerability was discovered and the whole fleet needed to be patched, we didn’t have a system that could say “go update every host at a safe rate.” We would literally recruit the whole team, subdivide all the hosts, and assign shifts. Everyone in the Cape Town office would get a chunk. Go update every one of your hosts, report status. That’s what life looks like without a mature control plane, and it’s the kind of thing that doesn’t scale. You can patch a fleet of a few hundred hosts that way. You cannot patch a fleet of millions that way. The control plane is what eventually got humans out of that loop entirely.

If you’ve lived through this progression, the scaling cliffs, the read replica tradeoffs, the sharding projects that always take longer than you think they will, you know it’s a long and painful road, and it’s one that every team building a successful service backed by a relational database eventually walks.

Searching for Database Xanadu

After a decade working on EC2, I formed some strong opinions on what my ideal database looks like. It scales with my business without heroics. It is highly available with no downtime for updates, and no servers to babysit. My ideal database lets me leverage the power of the relational data model to model my domain and write software more productively.

As it turns out, in the early 2020s, a group of experienced engineers on the databases side of AWS were thinking about exactly how to build this type of database. These engineers were expats from services like EC2 and had felt the pain of operating relational databases firsthand. They were also looking at the lessons learned operating massive scale serverless databases like DynamoDB and dreaming up ways to apply them to relational databases.

They wanted to do for databases what EC2 and really Lambda did to servers. If you operate a traditional database with a “head node” you are in the world of “servers with names” like I was before joining EC2. The ideal database would free you from thinking about “databases with names”. Instead, it would have a control plane that takes care of all of that for you so that you can just think about your database as a logical endpoint that’s always available while it scales up and down.

Sometime around 2021, this project really started to pick up steam. We’d figured out an architecture which seemed to deliver on this promise of the ideal database. I got the opportunity to join the team and start building its control plane. This service would launch in GA as Amazon Aurora DSQL in 2025.

Let’s quickly revisit the major pain points that EC2 went through and see how life is different on DSQL—especially for control plane builders.

In DSQL, there isn’t one server running your database. DSQL spins up a Firecracker micro-VM per connection, which means every connection is its own small head node. If one fails, only that single connection is affected rather than your whole application. Nobody gets paged, no one has to decide to cut over. I don’t manage standbys anymore, because the architecture has removed humans from that painful loop entirely.

Scaling reads was another problem we spent years on at EC2, adding replicas by hand and accepting eventual consistency as the cost. DSQL adds read replicas automatically, and in fact this is one of the primary jobs of the control plane that I helped build. If your application suddenly sees a spike in read traffic, DSQL handles it, and the reads are strongly consistent, always. After years of telling customers “try again in a moment,” this property still blows my mind. It fundamentally simplifies the architecture of any control plane built on DSQL, and it removes that cognitive tax from the developers using the APIs those control planes expose.

And then there’s sharding, which was availability zones and cells at EC2 and took us years. When you build AWS control planes for major new services, you have to anticipate that sharding will become necessary, and experience has shown that it’s cheaper to do it from the start than to retrofit it later. This is an ugly dilemma, because you’re extending your time to market on a speculative future problem, and when delivery timelines get tight, I’ve seen many teams give up on sharding just to ship. DSQL removes that dilemma because it automatically partitions your workload and you don’t have to think about it. You can use all the Postgres goodies you’re used to, complex transactions, multi-table joins, secondary indexes, while knowing your database is going to scale with your needs. Many new AWS control planes over the last decade were built on DynamoDB for this same reason, but DSQL offers a world with fewer compromises. You get the scalability of DynamoDB with the relational programming model that developers actually prefer to work with.

“Self-hosting”

When it came time to choose a database for the DSQL control plane, we chose DSQL. A team that runs on its own product feels every rough edge before its customers do, but getting there meant taking on the same circular dependency we’d faced at EC2: a control plane can’t depend on the thing it controls.

We’ve seen two significant benefits from the decision to “self-host”. As customers adopt DSQL, they are creating thousands of databases, and the control plane is continuously scaling their databases up and down based on usage, often very rapidly. All of this customer activity creates “bookkeeping” work for the DSQL control plane, and the amount of this work grows with DSQL adoption. Since the DSQL control plane runs on DSQL, our bookkeeping database scales up to keep up with this increase in demand with minimal work from the team.

The other benefit is in how we deal with availability zone outages. DSQL was designed from the ground up to survive single zone failures, but just because a zone is down doesn’t mean that customer workloads stop scaling or that customers stop creating databases. In my EC2 days, zone failures were fire storms as control plane databases died and pagers went off. For the DSQL control plane, these unfortunate bad days are much less painful because the DSQL control plane’s database remains available which allows the control plane to keep doing its critical work that ensures customer databases keep chugging along.

Taking off the rose-tinted glasses

If you’re still with me, you’re probably thinking to yourself: “what’s the catch?”

As a relatively new service, there are features that we just don’t support yet. Some of these are gaps that we’re actively filling. Others are more nuanced, and we want to take our time to make sure we build the right thing. A good example is foreign key constraints. Foreign key constraints are a classic database feature that can be very useful and aren’t fundamentally hard to implement. However, foreign keys can also be dangerous at scale. We want to get this right, and that takes time.

One of the advantages of running Postgres on a single node is that it maintains the working set in memory, and cached reads are insanely fast. Real architectures are more complicated though. For example, a control plane using Postgres would run across multiple availability zones and put a connection multiplexing proxy in front of the database. These are necessary steps for availability and scale, but they increase latency. When you build on DSQL, you don’t need to manage these things yourself. You get good (though not quite single-node Postgres good) latency that remains consistent as your application scales. This is exactly what I want as a control plane builder. Yes, I want fast, but I care even more about predictable latency as my application scales.

It’s also worth being honest about where things stand for control plane builders at AWS. Migrating something like EC2’s control plane onto DSQL would take years even if we started today, and that’s okay. The ten-odd years I spent on the EC2 control plane taught me that the work that matters most tends to measure its impact in years, not quarters.

Looking around corners

We’ve spent most of this post deep in database scaling and life support. It’s a familiar shape for a lot of engineering stories. The problems we faced at EC2, how to go faster without breaking things, how to spend more of our time on the things that matter to customers, how to coordinate across a team that grew from a handful of people to thousands, and how to keep the system reliable while the ground shifted underneath us, are the same problems every engineering organization runs into as it scales. They are close cousins of the problems that produced Amazon’s original distributed computing manifesto back in 1998, and my own focus narrowed over the years to a single version of them, which was how to let individual teams fully own a piece of EC2 and move fast on their most urgent problems without expensive coordination, all while the product still felt like one coherent thing to a customer.

When I look at the broader industry today, I see echoes of that same pressure playing out at a scale I did not expect, because the arrival of agentic coding has driven the cost of writing software down to almost nothing, and that pushes the hard part of the work somewhere else. When code is cheap, the bottleneck moves to judgment, to figuring out what to build, how to ship it safely, and how to anticipate what your customers will need before they ask. That is the same shift a good control plane makes for the people who build on it, taking the invisible work of keeping infrastructure alive off their plate so they can spend their attention on their customers, only now it is happening to software development as a whole, and even a single-person team feels the need to scale out.

I am not going to pretend I know what building software will look like a year from now, because we are in the middle of a remodel and the walls are still open. What I do know is that it is much easier to move fast when you are standing on a foundation that will not crack under you, and that the problems worth spending a career on have always been the ones that need your judgment rather than your ability to keep the bookkeeping layer from falling over. My hope is that DSQL gives the next generation of builders that foundation, and gives them back the time to go look around corners for their customers, which is the part I always wished we had more room for at EC2.

And as Werner says: “Now, go build.”

I don’t manage standbys anymore, because the architecture has removed humans from that painful loop entirely.Scaling reads was another problem we spent years on at EC2, adding replicas by hand and accepting eventual consistency as the cost. DSQL adds read replicas automatically, and in fact this is one of the primary jobs of the control plane that I helped build. If your application suddenly sees a spike in read traffic, DSQL handles it, and the reads are strongly consistent, always. After years of telling customers “try again in a moment,” this property still blows my mind. It fundamentally simplifies the architecture of any control plane built on DSQL, and it removes that cognitive tax from the developers using the APIs those control planes expose.And then there’s sharding, which was availability zones and cells at EC2 and took us years. When you build AWS control planes for major new services, you have to anticipate that sharding will become necessary, and experience has shown that it’s cheaper to do it from the start than to retrofit it later. This is an ugly dilemma, because you’re extending your time to market on a speculative future problem, and when delivery timelines get tight, I’ve seen many teams give up on sharding just to ship. DSQL removes that dilemma because it automatically partitions your workload and you don’t have to think about it. You can use all the Postgres goodies you’re used to, complex transactions, multi-table joins, secondary indexes, while knowing your database is going to scale with your needs. Many new AWS control planes over the last decade were built on DynamoDB for this same reason, but DSQL offers a world with fewer compromises. You get the scalability of DynamoDB with the relational programming model that developers actually prefer to work with.“Self-hosting” When it came time to choose a database for the DSQL control plane, we chose DSQL. A team that runs on its own product feels every rough edge before its customers do, but getting there meant taking on the same circular dependency we’d faced at EC2: a control plane can’t depend on the thing it controls.We’ve seen two significant benefits from the decision to “self-host”. As customers adopt DSQL, they are creating thousands of databases, and the control plane is continuously scaling their databases up and down based on usage, often very rapidly. All of this customer activity creates “bookkeeping” work for the DSQL control plane, and the amount of this work grows with DSQL adoption. Since the DSQL control plane runs on DSQL, our bookkeeping database scales up to keep up with this increase in demand with minimal work from the team.The other benefit is in how we deal with availability zone outages. DSQL was designed from the ground up to survive single zone failures, but just because a zone is down doesn’t mean that customer workloads stop scaling or that customers stop creating databases. In my EC2 days, zone failures were fire storms as control plane databases died and pagers went off. For the DSQL control plane, these unfortunate bad days are much less painful because the DSQL control plane’s database remains available which allows the control plane to keep doing its critical work that ensures customer databases keep chugging along.Taking off the rose-tinted glasses If you’re still with me, you’re probably thinking to yourself: “what’s the catch?”As a relatively new service, there are features that we just don’t support yet. Some of these are gaps that we’re actively filling. Others are more nuanced, and we want to take our time to make sure we build the right thing. A good example is foreign key constraints. Foreign key constraints are a classic database feature that can be very useful and aren’t fundamentally hard to implement. However, foreign keys can also be dangerous at scale. We want to get this right, and that takes time.One of the advantages of running Postgres on a single node is that it maintains the working set in memory, and cached reads are insanely fast. Real architectures are more complicated though. For example, a control plane using Postgres would run across multiple availability zones and put a connection multiplexing proxy in front of the database. These are necessary steps for availability and scale, but they increase latency. When you build on DSQL, you don’t need to manage these things yourself. You get good (though not quite single-node Postgres good) latency that remains consistent as your application scales. This is exactly what I want as a control plane builder. Yes, I want fast, but I care even more about predictable latency as my application scales.It’s also worth being honest about where things stand for control plane builders at AWS. Migrating something like EC2’s control plane onto DSQL would take years even if we started today, and that’s okay. The ten-odd years I spent on the EC2 control plane taught me that the work that matters most tends to measure its impact in years, not quarters.Looking around corners We’ve spent most of this post deep in database scaling and life support. It’s a familiar shape for a lot of engineering stories. The problems we faced at EC2, how to go faster without breaking things, how to spend more of our time on the things that matter to customers, how to coordinate across a team that grew from a handful of people to thousands, and how to keep the system reliable while the ground shifted underneath us, are the same problems every engineering organization runs into as it scales. They are close cousins of the problems that produced Amazon’s original distributed computing manifesto back in 1998, and my own focus narrowed over the years to a single version of them, which was how to let individual teams fully own a piece of EC2 and move fast on their most urgent problems without expensive coordination, all while the product still felt like one coherent thing to a customer.When I look at the broader industry today, I see echoes of that same pressure playing out at a scale I did not expect, because the arrival of agentic coding has driven the cost of writing software down to almost nothing, and that pushes the hard part of the work somewhere else. When code is cheap, the bottleneck moves to judgment, to figuring out what to build, how to ship it safely, and how to anticipate what your customers will need before they ask. That is the same shift a good control plane makes for the people who build on it, taking the invisible work of keeping infrastructure alive off their plate so they can spend their attention on their customers, only now it is happening to software development as a whole, and even a single-person team feels the need to scale out.I am not going to pretend I know what building software will look like a year from now, because we are in the middle of a remodel and the walls are still open. What I do know is that it is much easier to move fast when you are standing on a foundation that will not crack under you, and that the problems worth spending a career on have always been the ones that need your judgment rather than your ability to keep the bookkeeping layer from falling over. My hope is that DSQL gives the next generation of builders that foundation, and gives them back the time to go look around corners for their customers, which is the part I always wished we had more room for at EC2.And as Werner says: “Now, go build.”

The data plane is the set of core capabilities, the raw computing power, the hardware, the networking. The control plane is the conduit between those capabilities and customers. It’s the thing that takes what exists physically in a data center and presents it to you in a format you can actually consume and get value from. Without the control plane, you’d be back to SSH-ing into named servers in a closet somewhere. With it, you can spin up a thousand machines with an API call and never think about where they live.

Stripped down, EC2 lets you rent a virtual machine (VM) in the cloud, and the control plane’s job is to set up and tear down these VMs for you.

blocks.html_en: I like the analogy of a thermostat, because it’s constantly measuring the temperature, it knows where things need to be, and it’s always nudging the system in the right direction. That’s what our control plane does. It’s a continuous loop, watching the state of the world, comparing it to what should be true, and correcting the difference. When you launch a VM, the control plane records that a VM should exist, finds a physical server in the right data center, sets up the image, configures networking, and launches it. Later, if that server disappears for any reason, the control plane notices and updates its records to reflect reality. It’s always reconciling what is with what should be.

blocks.html_en: One thing the team talked about constantly, almost to the point where it became a mantra, was that no matter what happens to the control plane, VMs that are already running need to keep working. We call this static stability, and it sounds obvious because of course running VMs should keep running. But at scale, obvious things are the hardest to protect, because every new feature, every change, every dependency is a chance to accidentally violate that guarantee. Maintaining it is the difference between an outage where customers can’t launch new resources and an outage where everything stops. Both are bad, but the second is catastrophically worse. The fact that EC2 was statically stable gave me some comfort in my early days.

blocks.html_en: The simplest way things went wrong was also the scariest. Sometimes the primary database server just died. Our solution was a hot standby, a backup server continuously replicating from the primary, ideally only milliseconds behind. When the primary failed, we’d cut over to the standby and it could limit the outage to seconds. The team earned that through years of operational practice, building tooling, writing runbooks, training on-call engineers to execute the switchover under pressure. But seconds of outage still meant pagers getting lit up at 3am and asking humans to make decisions with incomplete information. We kept asking ourselves whether the architecture could take humans out of that loop entirely.

This is pretty frustrating when you think about it, because the data plane does all the heavy lifting, like downloading VM images, configuring networking, running workloads, while the database is just keeping track of what exists. Every instance we launched meant more inserts, more updates, and more reads against the database, and eventually the bookkeeper couldn’t keep up with the workers.

blocks.html_en: So we introduced more servers replicating from the primary and used these as read replicas. Many of the EC2 APIs don’t make any changes, they just describe the state of your current resources (how many VMs do you have, and so on). We sent traffic for these read-only APIs to our new read replicas and this massively reduced the load on our primary database server. This is standard practice for any team trying to scale up a relational database. Incidentally, this fleet of read replicas is why the EC2 API is eventually consistent, and as Marc Brooker has written, this puts an unfortunate cognitive load on our customers. It’s something we wanted to do better with DSQL, which we’ll get to in a bit.

blocks.html_en: Read replicas bought us time, but every write still funneled through a single primary server, and eventually we had to shard the database. The first phase of this was visible to customers as we split each AWS region into multiple availability zones (AZs), each with their own independent control plane and separate MySQL databases. This helped with both scaling and availability, since zones fail independently and the blast radius of any single failure shrinks. It also became a fundamental building block that allows AWS customers to build architectures resilient to the loss of a single AZ. The second phase was internal: we sharded each zone into what we call cells. Both of these projects took years of engineering time because they required changes across many services. Every place in the codebase that talks to the database has to know which shard to route to. Simple lookups by primary key are straightforward, but anything else, such as joins across data that doesn’t align with your sharding boundaries, gets much trickier. Even the simplest decisions have consequences at this level. Do you shard by account or by resource? Different services choose differently depending on their access patterns, and there’s no universally right answer.

blocks.html_en: There is also a human cost to all of this that I don’t think we talk about enough. In those early years, we didn’t have the automation to handle a lot of what a modern control plane just takes care of. When a security vulnerability was discovered and the whole fleet needed to be patched, we didn’t have a system that could say “go update every host at a safe rate.” We would literally recruit the whole team, subdivide all the hosts, and assign shifts. Everyone in the Cape Town office would get a chunk. Go update every one of your hosts, report status. That’s what life looks like without a mature control plane, and it’s the kind of thing that doesn’t scale. You can patch a fleet of a few hundred hosts that way. You cannot patch a fleet of millions that way. The control plane is what eventually got humans out of that loop entirely.

blocks.html_en: After a decade working on EC2, I formed some strong opinions on what my ideal database looks like. It scales with my business without heroics. It is highly available with no downtime for updates, and no servers to babysit. My ideal database lets me leverage the power of the relational data model to model my domain and write software more productively.

blocks.html_en: As it turns out, in the early 2020s, a group of experienced engineers on the databases side of AWS were thinking about exactly how to build this type of database. These engineers were expats from services like EC2 and had felt the pain of operating relational databases firsthand. They were also looking at the lessons learned operating massive scale serverless databases like DynamoDB and dreaming up ways to apply them to relational databases.

blocks.html_en: They wanted to do for databases what EC2 and really Lambda did to servers. If you operate a traditional database with a “head node” you are in the world of “servers with names” like I was before joining EC2. The ideal database would free you from thinking about “databases with names”. Instead, it would have a control plane that takes care of all of that for you so that you can just think about your database as a logical endpoint that’s always available while it scales up and down.

blocks.html_en: Let’s quickly revisit the major pain points that EC2 went through and see how life is different on DSQL—especially for control plane builders.

sentences.en: Let’s quickly revisit the major pain points that EC2 went through and see how life is different on DSQL—especially for control plane builders.
sentences.zh: 让我们快速回顾一下 EC2 经历的主要痛点，看看 DSQL 上的生活有何不同——尤其是对于控制平面构建者而言。

blocks.html_en: In DSQL, there isn’t one server running your database. DSQL spins up a Firecracker micro-VM per connection, which means every connection is its own small head node. If one fails, only that single connection is affected rather than your whole application. Nobody gets paged, no one has to decide to cut over. I don’t manage standbys anymore, because the architecture has removed humans from that painful loop entirely.

sentences.en: I don’t manage standbys anymore, because the architecture has removed humans from that painful loop entirely.
sentences.zh: 我不再管理备用数据库，因为该架构已将人类完全从这个痛苦的循环中移除。

blocks.html_en: Scaling reads was another problem we spent years on at EC2, adding replicas by hand and accepting eventual consistency as the cost. DSQL adds read replicas automatically, and in fact this is one of the primary jobs of the control plane that I helped build. If your application suddenly sees a spike in read traffic, DSQL handles it, and the reads are strongly consistent, always. After years of telling customers “try again in a moment,” this property still blows my mind. It fundamentally simplifies the architecture of any control plane built on DSQL, and it removes that cognitive tax from the developers using the APIs those control planes expose.

blocks.html_en: And then there’s sharding, which was availability zones and cells at EC2 and took us years. When you build AWS control planes for major new services, you have to anticipate that sharding will become necessary, and experience has shown that it’s cheaper to do it from the start than to retrofit it later. This is an ugly dilemma, because you’re extending your time to market on a speculative future problem, and when delivery timelines get tight, I’ve seen many teams give up on sharding just to ship. DSQL removes that dilemma because it automatically partitions your workload and you don’t have to think about it. You can use all the Postgres goodies you’re used to, complex transactions, multi-table joins, secondary indexes, while knowing your database is going to scale with your needs. Many new AWS control planes over the last decade were built on DynamoDB for this same reason, but DSQL offers a world with fewer compromises. blocks.html_en: When it came time to choose a database for the DSQL control plane, we chose DSQL. A team that runs on its own product feels every rough edge before its customers do, but getting there meant taking on the same circular dependency we’d faced at EC2: a control plane can’t depend on the thing it controls.

blocks.html_en: One of the advantages of running Postgres on a single node is that it maintains the working set in memory, and cached reads are insanely fast. For example, a control plane using Postgres would run across multiple availability zones and put a connection multiplexing proxy in front of the database. These are necessary steps for availability and scale, but they increase latency. When you build on DSQL, you don’t need to manage these things yourself. blocks.html_en: We’ve spent most of this post deep in database scaling and life support. It’s a familiar shape for a lot of engineering stories. The problems we faced at EC2, how to go faster without breaking things, how to spend more of our time on the things that matter to customers, how to coordinate across a team that grew from a handful of people to thousands, and how to keep the system reliable while the ground shifted underneath us, are the same problems every engineering organization runs into as it scales. They are close cousins of the problems that produced Amazon’s original distributed computing manifesto back in 1998, and my own focus narrowed over the years to a single version of them, which was how to let individual teams fully own a piece of EC2 and move fast on their most urgent problems without expensive coordination, all while the product still felt like one coherent thing to a customer.

content_html_zh:
2026 年 8 月 4 日 • 3756 字

Zak van der Merwe 的整个职业生涯都在 AWS 构建控制平面上度过。 首先用于 EC2，现在用于 DSQL。 从表面上看，控制平面看起来很无聊：它记录应该存在的内容，并将其与实际执行的内容相协调。 没有人离开学校时梦想着构建一个系统，但扎克将第一个告诉你，如果你喜欢解决分布式系统中的难题，那么没有比这更好的地方了。 这是许多难题的汇聚点，也是您做出的决策决定服务能否持续发展的地方。

如果您一直在关注 Marc Brooker 和 Marc Bowes 关于 DSQL 的文章，那么这是一篇很棒的姊妹篇，它拉开了帷幕，展示了构建从一开始就考虑到控制平面工程师的数据库的意义。

–W

关于构建可扩展的控制平面

我在 AWS 工作了近 14 年，几乎所有时间我都在构建控制平面。 这不是任何人为自己规划的职业。 离开大学时，没有人会想“我想在接下来的十年里确保云服务的簿记层保持正常运行。” 但我在这里，我认为我还在这里的原因是控制平面是许多有趣问题存在的地方，即使需要一段时间才能清楚地看到这一点。

在加入亚马逊之前，我在开普敦的一家电信公司工作，那里大约有十台服务器，全部都在办公室后面的一个房间里，每台服务器都有一个名字。 你可以通过 SSH 连接到它们，与你的同事分享它们，如果出现问题，你可以走过去处理它。 这就是我对运行基础设施意味着什么的整个心智模型。 服务器是你单独了解、精心维护的东西，并且可以作为一个整体进行推理，因为数量很少，足以容纳你的头脑。

我提到这一点并不是因为这是一个不寻常的背景，而是因为它在不到二十年前非常普遍，我认为这就是值得大声说出来的原因。 也许您的版本是一个小型 Kubernetes 集群或几个 RDS 实例，您可以在其中可视化整个事物，可以命名各个部分，并且当出现问题时您知道哪个部分出现问题。 了解您的基础设施的感觉很舒服，这使得故事的下一部分真正难以描述，因为当我加入 EC2 时，这种感觉就消失了。

老实说，当我开始时，我并不太了解 EC2 是如何工作的。 我一直试图将其映射回我所知道的。 如果我启动一个实例并且底层服务器挂掉了，会发生什么？ 我的虚拟机是否会以某种方式传送到另一台主机上？ 云如何营造出硬件故障无关紧要的错觉？ 我无法将其中的任何内容与我对运行软件的了解联系起来。

我在 EC2 的第一份工作是对机群进行健康检查，对每台服务器执行 ping 操作，并尝试确定其是否健康，但我的发现却与魔法相反。 事情不断失败。 主机出现故障、硬件出现故障、磁盘出现故障。 我已经看到了 EC2 的弱点，它是混乱的。 我的思维模式已经从“服务器是你保护的宝贵东西”变成了“一切都一直在着火”。

我花了一段时间才摆脱这种感觉，但我最终意识到，这些失败只是工作正常的巨大海洋中的微小滴。 该系统只是在一定范围内运行，故障是一种常态，一种统计上的确定性，而不是一种紧急情况。 控制平面使得运行如此规模的服务成为可能，而无需人工对每次故障做出响应，并使一切保持正常运转。

无论如何，我在 AWS 的这些年都是在控制平面上工作的。 每项 AWS 服务都有一个，我喜欢将他们视为我们的无名英雄。 他们工作得越好，人们就越少注意到他们。 它们是您不必为服务器命名的原因，也是当硬件发生故障时，您作为客户永远不必处理它的原因。 我已经为两个主要的 AWS 服务构建了控制平面：EC2 和 DSQL。 它们相隔近十年，但建造一个的惨痛教训直接导致了另一个的设计，这就是我今天想讲的故事。

到底什么是控制平面？

在这一点上，我可能欠你一个更好的解释，解释我所说的控制平面是什么意思，以及为什么我认为它们很有趣。 我将使用 EC2 作为示例，因为我在那里学到了大部分知识。

我的想法是每个服务都有一个数据平面和一个控制平面。 数据平面是核心功能、原始计算能力、硬件、网络的集合。 控制平面是这些功能和客户之间的渠道。 它采用数据中心中物理存在的内容，并以您可以实际使用并从中获取价值的格式呈现给您。 如果没有控制平面，您将不得不通过 SSH 连接到某处壁橱中的指定服务器。 有了它，您可以通过 API 调用启动一千台机器，而无需考虑它们位于何处。

EC2 涉及数千名工程师和比任何人都可以跟踪的更多功能，但从概念上讲，控制平面...... 很简单。 简单来说，EC2 允许您在云中租用虚拟机 (VM)，而控制平面的工作就是为您设置和拆除这些 VM。

我喜欢恒温器的类比，因为它不断测量温度，它知道事情需要在哪里，并且总是将系统推向正确的方向。 这就是我们的控制平面所做的。 这是一个连续的循环，观察世界的状况，将其与真实情况进行比较，并纠正差异。 当您启动虚拟机时，控制平面会记录虚拟机应该存在的信息，在正确的数据中心找到物理服务器，设置映像，配置网络，然后启动它。 稍后，如果该服务器因任何原因消失，控制平面会注意到并更新其记录以反映现实。 它总是使现状与应该的相协调。

团队不断谈论的一件事，几乎成为了口头禅，那就是，无论控制平面发生什么情况，已经运行的虚拟机都需要继续工作。 我们称之为静态稳定性，这听起来很明显，因为运行中的虚拟机当然应该保持运行。 但从规模上看，显而易见的东西是最难保护的，因为每一个新功能、每一个变化、每一个依赖项都有可能意外违反这一保证。 维护它是客户无法启动新资源的中断和一切都停止的中断之间的区别。 两者都很糟糕，但第二个更糟糕。 EC2 静态稳定这一事实给我在早期带来了一些安慰。

EC2 团队做了出色的工作，让糟糕的日子不再发生。 但了解糟糕的日子是什么样子塑造了我对构建控制平面的很多了解。

生活在控制平面内

要了解糟糕的日子是如何开始的，了解控制平面如何存储状态会有所帮助。 EC2 控制平面的核心是一个关系数据库。 当客户调用 RunInstances API 启动虚拟机时，最关键的事情是控制平面将一行写入其数据库：客户 X 现在拥有虚拟机 Y。 那时 API 可以安全返回。

实际上，单个 RunInstances 请求会触发微服务和宏服务之间的数百或数千个内部 API 调用。 其中许多服务都有自己的数据库记录自己的状态。 很难夸大这些年来它变得多么复杂，但在所有这些复杂性的最底层，有一个 MySQL 数据库，并且该数据库中的内容应该与现实相符。

事情出错的最简单方式也是最可怕的。 有时主数据库服务器就死掉了。 我们的解决方案是热备用，即备份服务器不断从主服务器进行复制，最好只落后几毫秒。 当主服务器发生故障时，我们会切换到备用服务器，这样可以将中断时间限制在几秒钟之内。 该团队通过多年的运营实践、构建工具、编写操作手册、培训待命工程师在压力下执行切换而获得了这一点。 但几秒钟的停电仍然意味着寻呼机会在凌晨 3 点亮起，要求人们在信息不完整的情况下做出决定。 我们不断地问自己，这个架构是否可以让人类完全摆脱这个循环。

更慢、更长期的问题是确保我们的 MySQL 数据库跟上业务增长。 仔细想想，这是相当令人沮丧的，因为数据平面承担了所有繁重的工作，例如下载虚拟机​​映像、配置网络、运行工作负载，而数据库只是跟踪存在的内容。 我们启动的每个实例都意味着对数据库进行更多的插入、更新和读取，最终簿记员无法跟上工作人员的速度。

因此，我们引入了更多从主服务器进行复制的服务器，并将它们用作只读副本。 许多 EC2 API 不进行任何更改，它们只是描述当前资源的状态（您有多少个虚拟机，等等）。 我们将这些只读 API 的流量发送到新的只读副本，这大大减少了主数据库服务器上的负载。 对于任何尝试扩展关系数据库的团队来说，这是标准做法。 顺便说一句，这组只读副本就是 EC2 API 最终保持一致的原因，正如 Marc Brooker 所写，这给我们的客户带来了不幸的认知负担。 这是我们希望使用 DSQL 做得更好的事情，我们稍后会谈到。

只读副本为我们赢得了时间，但每次写入仍然通过单个主服务器进行，​​最终我们不得不对数据库进行分片。 第一阶段对客户来说是可见的，因为我们将每个 AWS 区域划分为多个可用区 (AZ)，每个可用区都有自己独立的控制平面和单独的 MySQL 数据库。 这有助于扩展和可用性，因为区域独立发生故障并且任何单个故障的影响半径都会缩小。 它还成为一个基本构建块，使 AWS 客户能够构建能够抵御单个可用区丢失的架构。 第二阶段是内部阶段：我们将每个区域划分为我们所说的单元。 这两个项目都花费了数年的工程时间，因为它们需要对许多服务进行更改。 代码库中与数据库通信的每个位置都必须知道要路由到哪个分片。 通过主键进行简单查找很简单，但其他任何事情（例如与分片边界不符的数据之间的联接）都会变得更加棘手。 即使是最简单的决定也会在这个层面上产生后果。 您是按帐户还是按资源进行分片？ 不同的服务根据其访问模式做出不同的选择，并且没有普遍正确的答案。

所有这一切还带来了人力成本，我认为我们对此讨论得还不够。 在早年，我们没有自动化来处理现代控制平面所处理的许多事情。 当发现安全漏洞并且需要修补整个机群时，我们没有一个系统可以说“以安全的速度更新每台主机”。 我们实际上会招募整个团队，细分所有主持人并分配轮班。 开普敦办公室的每个人都会得到一大笔。 去更新每台主机，报告状态。 这就是没有成熟控制平面的生活的样子，而且是无法扩展的事情。 您可以通过这种方式修补由数百台主机组成的队列。 你无法通过这种方式修补数以百万计的车队。 控制平面最终使人类完全摆脱了这个循环。

如果您经历过这一过程、扩展悬崖、只读副本权衡、总是比您想象的时间更长的分片项目，您就会知道这是一条漫长而痛苦的道路，也是每个构建由关系数据库支持的成功服务的团队最终都会走的一条路。

搜索数据库 Xanadu

在 EC2 上工作了十年之后，我对我的理想数据库形成了一些强烈的看法。 它可以与我的业务一起扩展，无需英雄主义。 它具有高可用性，无需停机更新，也无需托管服务器。 我理想的数据库让我能够利用关系数据模型的强大功能来对我的领域进行建模并更高效地编写软件。

事实证明，在 2020 年代初期，AWS 数据库方面的一群经验丰富的工程师正在思考如何构建此类数据库。 这些工程师是来自 EC2 等服务的外籍人士，亲身体验过操作关系数据库的痛苦。 他们还研究了操作 DynamoDB 等大规模无服务器数据库的经验教训，并想出将其应用于关系数据库的方法。

他们希望为数据库做 EC2 和 Lambda 对服务器所做的事情。 如果您使用“头节点”操作传统数据库，那么您就处于“有名称的服务器”的世界中，就像我在加入 EC2 之前一样。 理想的数据库将使您摆脱“有名称的数据库”的思考。 相反，它会有一个控制平面来为您处理所有这些事情，这样您就可以将数据库视为一个逻辑端点，在扩展和缩小时始终可用。

2021 年左右的某个时候，这个项目真正开始加速发展。 我们已经找到了一种架构，它似乎能够兑现理想数据库的承诺。 我有机会加入该团队并开始构建其控制平面。 该服务将于 2025 年以 Amazon Aurora DSQL 正式发布。

让我们快速回顾一下 EC2 经历的主要痛点，看看 DSQL 上的生活有何不同——尤其是对于控制平面构建者而言。

在 DSQL 中，没有一台服务器运行您的数据库。 DSQL 为每个连接启动一个 Firecracker 微虚拟机，这意味着每个连接都是它自己的小头节点。 如果其中一个失败，则只有该单个连接受到影响，而不是整个应用程序受到影响。 没有人被寻呼，没有人必须决定切换。 我不再管理备用数据库，因为该架构已将人类完全从这个痛苦的循环中移除。

扩展读取是我们在 EC2 花费多年时间解决的另一个问题，手动添加副本并接受最终一致性作为成本。 DSQL 自动添加只读副本，事实上，这是我帮助构建的控制平面的主要工作之一。 如果您的应用程序突然发现读取流量激增，DSQL 会处理它，并且读取始终保持高度一致。 经过多年告诉顾客“稍后再试”之后，这家酒店仍然让我震惊。 它从根本上简化了基于 DSQL 构建的任何控制平面的架构，并且消除了使用这些控制平面公开的 API 的开发人员的认知负担。

然后是分片，即 EC2 上的可用区域和单元，我们花了数年时间。 当您为主要新服务构建 AWS 控制平面时，您必须预见到分片将变得必要，并且经验表明，从一开始就这样做比稍后进行改造要便宜。 这是一个丑陋的困境，因为你要在一个推测性的未来问题上延长上市时间，而当交付时间紧迫时，我看到许多团队为了交付而放弃分片。 DSQL 消除了这种困境，因为它会自动划分您的工作负载，而您无需考虑它。 您可以使用您习惯的所有 Postgres 功能、复杂事务、多表连接、二级索引，同时知道您的数据库将根据您的需求进行扩展。 出于同样的原因，过去十年中许多新的 AWS 控制平面都是在 DynamoDB 上构建的，但 DSQL 提供了一个更少妥协的世界。 您可以通过开发人员实际更喜欢使用的关系编程模型获得 DynamoDB 的可扩展性。

“自托管”

当需要为 DSQL 控制平面选择数据库时，我们选择了 DSQL。 一个运行自己产品的团队比客户更先感受到每一个粗糙的边缘，但到达那里意味着要承担我们在 EC2 中面临的相同循环依赖：控制平面不能依赖于它控制的东西。

我们看到“自我托管”的决定有两个显着的好处。 当客户采用 DSQL 时，他们会创建数千个数据库，并且控制平面会根据使用情况不断扩展和缩减数据库，而且速度通常非常快。 所有这些客户活动都会为 DSQL 控制平面创建“簿记”工作，并且这项工作的量随着 DSQL 的采用而增加。 由于 DSQL 控制平面在 DSQL 上运行，因此我们的簿记数据库可以扩展，以跟上需求的增长，而团队只需要做最少的工作。

另一个好处是我们如何处理可用区中断。 DSQL 的设计初衷是为了应对单区域故障，但仅仅因为一个区域发生故障并不意味着客户工作负载停止扩展或客户停止创建数据库。 在我的 EC2 时代，区域故障就像一场火灾风暴，因为控制平面数据库崩溃并且寻呼机关闭。 对于 DSQL 控制平面来说，这些不幸的糟糕日子要少得多，因为 DSQL 控制平面的数据库仍然可用，这允许控制平面继续执行其关键工作，确保客户数据库保持正常运行。

摘掉玫瑰色眼镜

如果你还和我在一起，你可能会想：“有什么问题吗？”

作为一项相对较新的服务，我们尚不支持某些功能。 其中一些是我们正在积极填补的空白。 其他的则更加微妙，我们希望花时间确保我们构建正确的东西。 一个很好的例子是外键约束。 外键约束是一个经典的数据库功能，非常有用，而且从根本上来说实现起来并不困难。 然而，外键在大规模时也可能是危险的。 我们想要把这件事做好，这需要时间。

在单个节点上运行 Postgres 的优点之一是它在内存中维护工作集，并且缓存的读取速度非常快。 但实际的架构要复杂得多。 例如，使用 Postgres 的控制平面将跨多个可用区运行，并在数据库前面放置一个连接多路复用代理。 这些是可用性和规模的必要步骤，但它们会增加延迟。 当您基于 DSQL 进行构建时，您不需要自己管理这些事情。 您可以获得良好的延迟（尽管不如单节点 Postgres 那样好），并且随着应用程序的扩展而保持一致。 这正是我作为控制平面构建者想要的。 是的，我想要快速，但我更关心随着应用程序扩展的可预测延迟。

诚实地了解 AWS 控制平面构建者的情况也是值得的。 即使我们今天开始，将 EC2 的控制平面之类的东西迁移到 DSQL 也需要数年时间，但这没关系。 我在 EC2 控制平面上度过的十多年告诉我，最重要的工作往往以年而不是季度来衡量其影响。

环视角落

我们在这篇文章中花了大部分时间来深入探讨数据库扩展和生命支持。 这是许多工程故事中熟悉的形状。 我们在 EC2 面临的问题是，如何在不破坏事物的情况下加快速度，如何将更多时间花在对客户重要的事情上，如何在从少数人发展到数千人的团队中进行协调，以及如何在地面发生变化时保持系统可靠，这些都是每个工程组织在扩展时遇到的相同问题。 它们与 1998 年 Amazon 最初的分布式计算宣言所面临的问题非常相似，多年来我自己的关注点缩小到了它们的一个版本，即如何让各个团队完全拥有 EC2 的一部分，并在无需昂贵的协调的情况下快速解决最紧迫的问题，同时产品对客户来说仍然感觉是一个连贯的东西。

当我审视今天更广泛的行业时，我看到同样的压力以我意想不到的规模出现，因为代理编码的到来使编写软件的成本几乎降到了零，这将工作的困难部分推到了其他地方。 当代码很便宜时，瓶颈就会转移到判断上，转移到弄清楚要构建什么、如何安全地交付它以及如何在客户提出要求之前预测他们需要什么。 这与良好的控制平面为在其上构建的人们带来的转变相同，将保持基础设施运行的无形工作从他们的工作中解放出来，以便他们可以将注意力集中在客户身上，只是现在它正在发生在整个软件开发中，甚至单人团队也觉得有必要进行扩展。

我不会假装我知道一年后的建筑软件会是什么样子，因为我们正处于改造过程中，而且墙壁仍然开放。 我所知道的是，当你站在一个不会在你脚下破裂的基础上时，快速行动会容易得多，并且值得花费一生时间解决的问题始终是需要你的判断力的问题，而不是你防止簿记层倒塌的能力。 我希望 DSQL 为下一代构建者提供这样的基础，并让他们有时间四处寻找客户，这是我一直希望我们在 EC2 拥有更多空间的部分。

正如沃纳所说：“现在，开始建造吧。”
